What was your practice routine like?
Oh, practice...
I’m talking about then, the ‘40s, the ‘50s...

I was working a lot then. I didn’t have no practice routine. When I started playing a lot, I never practiced, because I’d just go to work. If I got tired of playing a song, I just played it another key or something like that. Keep myself fresh. It made me think about what I’m doing.
Back to alto players, did you get to know Jackie McLean well?
I knew Jackie McLean well. He was like a brother.
When did you meet him? When you got to New York?

Yeah. I lived up there. I lived on 155th. He lived on 158th. Sonny Rollins lived around the corner. Edgecombe Avenue. I’d see all of them. But these guys were junkies. They were junkies. Sorry to say, but I had no use for no junkies. Because I thought it would just be my luck to be talking to one of them and the police run up and get us—get everybody.
You thought you’d be caught in the same net, you mean?
You got it. Because all they did was hustle every day to try to get money, to get high. They had some musical talent. But they’re characters that I wouldn’t recommend.
Now, people did change and get over their habits.
I don’t know. I doubt it.
When did you first meet someone who was strung out on drugs?
When did I first MEET someone?
Yeah. In North Carolina?

Oh, no. No drugs in North Carolina. They’d give you thirty years for smoking weed down there. They didn’t have no junkies in North Carolina, not when I was there. When I got to New York, I saw plenty of junkies.
So your attitude towards people who were abusing drugs was more based on self- preservation, it sounds like, than anything else...

Well, actually, none of them played as well as they thought they was playing when they was high. I could have got somebody sober to play better. Because everybody was following Trane. But Trane jumped the track, and they jumped it right behind him. Now all of them are unemployed. I call that “unemployment music.” And they still play it. Disk jockeys and record companies are so stupid. They don’t even acknowledge it because they’re stupid.
Elaborate.

Well, that’s a style of music that you can’t play in Atlanta. Charlotte, North Carolina. Birmingham. Big cities. St. Louis. You can’t play a steady gig there playing that. Kansas City. All the big cities. You can play it in New York, maybe one joint in Chicago— although Joe Segal has now started mixing up his entertainment. Nowhere in California can you play it, not on a steady gig. And that’s very counter-productive.
Back to alto players. Phil Woods was the fourth name I wrote down here. Were you and he friends in the ‘50s?

Oh, yeah. I like Phil. I like Phil very well, because Phil was one of the few white guys that, when he got famous, he didn’t forget the black guys. A lot of the white guys, once they got famous, made a couple of records and ran all off with the white bands. But Phil always kept some brothers around. Well, I guess he wanted the feeling in his band.

Another alto player I can think of in the ‘50s who had his own sound was Lee Konitz. I recall when we did the DownBeat Blindfold Test, I gave you a track by him, and you had some interesting things to change.

Yeah, I know Lee Konitz. Lee Konitz is a sax-o-phon-ist. I wouldn’t call him exactly a great jazz player, but he’s a good saxophone player. Him and Paul Desmond, too. They sound like they’re playing clarinets. They don’t even have the sound.
So for you, it’s very important to have...

I mean, a SOUND. A bluesy sound. They don’t have it. They can’t play the blues, unfortunately. They play what they’re playing. But the blues, a different thing. And if you can’t play blues, you can’t play jazz, period. Now, if you can play it and don’t play it, you’re still not playing jazz—period. I listen to all the stuff Coltrane’s playing. No blues. In fact, I did a survey... I didn’t do a survey. Mark Elf, guitar player. I had him to monitor the public commercial radio stations. He got the best tune that was hot, something by 50 Cents or somebody, and he monitored that tune for a week. You know how much airplay they got?
How much?
715 times. And I had to monitor Coltrane and see how much airplay he got on a commercial station. You know how many he got?
How many?
[RAISES HAND WITH INDEX FINGER AND THUMB IN A CIRCLE, AND THREE FINGERS OUTSTRETCHED]
That’s three. Oh, it’s zero.

That’s zero! Not one. Now, that’s no good. You can’t even stay in business like that. Because you know, and anybody else knows, that years and years and years, we got a lot of play on commercial stations with Duke Ellington’s tunes and Count Basie, “April in Paris” and all that kind of stuff. We got play on commercial stations. But now jazz...kiss it goodbye. TV? I haven’t seen a jazz show since Tony Bennett was on there years ago, and brought Count Basie on there.

I’m going to move into another area. You were one of the first jazz group leaders to use a conga player, as you were describing with Ray Barretto on those Blue Note dates from 1957. I think you used the phrase just now, “straighten out the rhythm.” What exactly did you mean by that, and what...

Actually, I meant control. Now you can see today you’ve got these guys like Poncho Sanchez and a couple of more Latino musicians making a lot of money, because they put that beat with jazz. Because there’s no such thing as Latin Jazz. You can kiss that goodbye. That’s a misnomer. It’s jazz with Latin rhythm. That’s all it is. And when they keep that rhythm, which is the heart of the thinking in their music, they can sell the records. We could have done it ourselves if we’d kept our rhythm, with Kenny Clarke and Max... Those guys were shooting a little cocaine...shooting a little heroin and snorting a little cocaine—they didn’t want to swing any more. They wanted to take a solo. Most of the time, when somebody else is soloing. That’s what the problem is. That’s how they’re losing out.
But what was the value for you of having the conga player?
To steady down the rhythm. That’s all.
You had done a date in 1955 with Gene Ammons. It’s the one sideman recording with you that I know of from that period. I know that he also liked to use the congas.
Yes.
He used it a lot. Were you friendly with him?
Yes.

And they all played music, too?
Yes, they played music.

Oh, yeah. I listened to them. I listened to them on radio. I told you we had a short­ wave radio. We could pick it up late at night down in the South. We’d pick them up. When they got to 12 o’clock, we couldn’t...

that was during the war.

The South, yeah.

You couldn’t say anything about it. She wouldn’t let you do it. I never heard her say a bad word about anybody. Now, of course, that’s different from me. That’s one characteristic I didn’t pick up. Heh-heh...

Of course. Religious. Very religious. She went to church four times every Sunday.

That’s right. I told my father, once I get away from here, that’s it.

Oh, no. I got the information. She gave me information about everything.

What was your father’s style of preaching?

In between what?

Of course. The time, the tempo, the rhythm, the building up of like a solo—all of that goes into it. And such wonderful singers. You never heard such wonderful singers in all of your life.

Actually, I was trying to emulate Johnny Hodges and those kind of people. I wasn’t really trying to emulate the church. Because I knew all of the... Just stepping back again, was there any blues in town as a kid?
In my town? Yeah, people would sing blues.

You described the extraction process yesterday.
Yes.

No-no.

So he made a quick impression.
A big impression. I wanted to play like that.

So it made you want to find out what he was doing...
Find out what he was doing and play the same way. Play it the same way, if possible.
How did you measure yourself in that regard? Did you just listen to the records over and over and over, and wear them out until you...

That’s what I did. Listened to the record. I’d wind the record down to the aluminum base. They had an aluminum base. I’d cut it down. And when I couldn’t get the phrases, I’d put it down to 33-1/3 speed. It would be in another key, but you could still get the phrases. If you cut it down, he sounded like Lester Young—if you cut down the speed.

I got them from the guys in Chicago. See, some guys in my band came from Chicago, and they brought the records out to the base, and they’d be playing them?

Oh, no-no.
“Red Cross”? Or before that.
No. Way before that. Wasn’t nothing like that out.

Everything with McShann. So your experience with Charlie Parker...
Was with McShann.

Of course. Stayed on everything.

So you could use your imagination and creativity that way, by finding out the connections.
Of course. Once I learned to resolve chords, go from one chord to another, I’d just
buy the sheet music and I could see where the chords went.

Billy Tolles was from Seattle, right?
Seattle, Washington. He was a great saxophone player. He could play all that kind of stuff when he came down to North Carolina.

No, we played in clubs. And we played bebop. We played a regular show, then we’d play bebop. You had to play a regular show first. Then we’d play some bebop tunes.
You mean at the end of the show.
At the end of the show.
Now, you said that’s been your m.o. ever since.
Yes.

You didn’t tell me that.
I had to go to the music shop to buy a saxophone. I didn’t tell you that?
No.

I was in there, so I started to play the... [SINGS REFRAIN OF “GROOVIN’ HIGH”] All of a sudden, I hear this guitar player over there playing the same thing I was playing. Yeah.

Oh, my great-grandfather. He built St. Paul University. He built the buildings. He was a mason and a carpenter.

It had to be in the 1920s.

Yes.

well, maybe my grandfather. My mother’s father. That’s who it was. My grandfather. A lot of my mother’s sisters taught in the college.

Talk about that a bit.

Hard-working man. Where was he from?

Herman Foster or Horace Parlan were the pianists...
George Tucker and Al Harewood.
Also Peck Morrison and Dave Bailey.
Right.

Well, for me, they weren’t junkies. That’s why I used them. Because like I told you, I told Alfred Lion junkies had to go.
But how about as far as what they did musically?

Well, we played around New York together. I’d see them all the time. We had two or three places we played, and then we had one place we’d play every night called Connie’s. You mean the breakfast session.
Yes.

Every night. Right across the street was Roy Campanella’s liquor store. In fact, Leo Durocher was over there one time. We got to meet all the ballplayers.
I guess the New York Giants were Harlem’s team.

Of course. The New York Giants. And the Brooklyn Dodgers. They loved the Dodgers, too. I was there the night Campanella got hurt. [January 27, 1958] What happened... This is an amazing story. I was in Small’s Paradise. Wilt Chamberlain owned it at that time. I was over there talking to Wilt, and Campanella came in there because once... He closed up about 1 o’clock, and Wilt stayed open til about 4. There was a girl, a barmaid that Roy liked, so he came over, but it was snowing a little bit, not much... So I drove my car in low gear from Harlem all the way right to this house in the Bronx. When I got in, I was so late... If I had to go down some curves, I wouldn’t have any gone anywhere either. That’s amazing. Amazing story.

Oh, yeah. Everybody.
In the black community mostly, but some in the white community, too.

Working.
Working or looking. When I wasn’t working, I was looking. I met everybody. Everybody you probably can name, I met them.
Wilt Chamberlain bought his interest in Smalls when? 1961? 1962?

So you were working for him.
Sometimes. Not all the time.

I worked at the Club Barron. I worked at Count Basie’s. He had a club. I worked down at the Baby Grand sometimes. Another place called the Top Club.
About how many days a week would you say you were working from 1955 to the late ‘60s? 300 days a year?
No, not that much. I wouldn’t work that much. There was three or four clubs out in Long Island I worked, too. Bop City and two more clubs out there I used to work.
Brooklyn, too, I would think.
Yeah, Brooklyn... I used to work the Baby Grand over there, and I used to work Scotty’s Club over there, and that other club on Fulton and Nostrand.
Oh, not the Blue Coronet...
The Blue Coronet. That was a tough club.
Tough in terms of the clientele?
That’s right. You had a few fights now and then.
Again, talking about the band, do the Blue Note recordings from 1957-1958-1959, like Blues Walk or Sunny Side Up reflect what your band was playing in those clubs?
No. Because I used all that on those things... I wasn’t even playing organ in those clubs.
On Sunny Side Up you used piano. Horace Parlan.
Oh, ok. Maybe I did. I went on the road with that group, Horace Parlan, George Tucker and Al Harewood, and I had Tommy Turrentine on trumpet.
So the records were not a direct reflection of what you would do in the club.
Unh-uh.
How would it be different?

Well, when they wanted a date, I’d just figure out something to do to make it. I’d change the personnel according to what I was playing at that time. What I used to do, I used to play... If I was going to make a date, two weeks before I made it, I’d play the tunes in the club to see what kind of response I got, and the ones I didn’t get a response to, I didn’t record, and I was home free. Because everything I made during that time, sold.
Probably a lot of ‘78s also at that time.
Many ‘78s.
For the jukebox trade.
Yeah, many ‘78s.
When you started carrying an organ, it’s about 1960...
Yeah, something like that.
The first organist you traveled with extensively was John Patton, although you’d been doing some gigs with Jimmy Smith before that.
Yeah, John Patton was the first one I took on the road.
How did you meet?

Now, in the ‘80s, it seems like the climate changed somewhat because of the infusion of young musicians who were interested in playing the music...who paid attention to the hardcore jazz tradition. It got more acoustic in some ways. Wynton Marsalis had something to do with it, but also Art Blakey brought all these guys into the Jazz Messengers. And you’ve kept track of the young alto players who emerged during that time, like Donald Harrison, Kenny Garrett, Vincent Herring...
Right.

What’s your impression of that... Well, they’re not young any more; they’re middle- aged, in their forties and fifties. But your impression of that particular period and how things played out with that group of alto players. Your sense of the state of the alto saxophone these days.
Well, back in those days, see, Art Blakey had those Messengers... That was like a scam band. He did that so he could keep his habit going. He wasn’t interested in promoting no

musicians. He talked it all the time, but he wasn’t. Because the reason all of them quit was as soon as one of them would ask him about the money, he’d get another one. [LAUGHS] See, I know that, but the critics don’t know that.
Nonetheless, it did wind up being probably beneficial in the long run for these guys to have the chance to do that.
For some of those musicians. Yeah, Wynton got famous with that. Wynton got famous with that, and he’s still famous.
But apart from that band, just your sense of this group of musicians who started to emerge then? Was it a healthy thing for the music? Did it change the climate?

Well, it’s always healthy when somebody new comes in. Because it’s like new blood. It’s always healthy. But what happens is that you get so many people... Lee Morgan was one of them, too. You get so many people until you can’t...you got a whole lot of chiefs and no Indians. Because when they leave Art, they want to get a band. So what you got is a lot of bands, but no musicians, and no real definite sound. Now, you notice that nobody, even now, is dominant. What’s the alto saxophone player that’s dominant? I mean, other than Kenny G. David Sanborn. No jazz alto saxophone player is dominant.
What do you make of that? Too many chiefs, no Indians, or...
Well, not necessarily that. It’s because all of them come through the same thing, and they’re not playing anything, because all of them are playing the same.
Is that because of the way jazz education is now? Coming up in conservatories and not bands?

Well, partly. Partly. Partly. But anybody who comes through school and learns all the basics, they got to know that everybody is not supposed to sound the same. If you go through the school and learn the basics, you know that.

Well, they have to sound a little different. When we did the Blindfold Test, you told them all apart. You could pinpoint who Donald Harrison was, and who Kenny Garrett was, and who Vincent Herring was...

Yeah. Well, still you got to... Right now, I don’t know. Nobody is dominant. We did a survey, which the critics don’t know about. A cat bet me $100 that... I wouldn’t disagree.

Well, you know what Branch Rickey said.
Yes.
“Luck is the residue of design.”

Yup. Yup. But, see, music... Let me tell you something about music before you cut this off. You talk about Wynton. Now, Wynton did something that is very hard to do.
